text: Obed-Edom can mean "servant of the red." Edom shares its root with dam, blood. His secret was the blood on the mercy seat.
explanation:
After Uzzah died, David was afraid and left the ark at the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite for three months, "and the Lord blessed Obed-Edom and all his household." Scripture doesn't say why. But Edom, like Adam, comes from the Hebrew root for red, and dam is the word for blood. Obed means servant.

He likely understood what Uzzah never grasped: we approach God's presence only on the basis of shed blood. "It is the blood that makes atonement for the soul." Obed-Edom deserved death as much as Uzzah, but under the blood God saw him as righteous and blessed him that way. You have a far greater sacrifice: the blood of Jesus, shed once for all.

text: When David came back for the ark, something was new: every six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fatted sheep.
explanation:
There had been music and worship on the first attempt too, right up until the oxen stumbled. Praise wasn't what was missing. On the second journey, "when those bearing the ark of the Lord had gone six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fatted sheep." Picture columns of smoke rising all along the road to Zion.

It's the first time we see David offering sacrifices for the ark, and he may have learned it from watching Obed-Edom. That's how God often draws people back: they see His goodness on someone's household and remember what they've lost. Let the blood of Jesus be your confidence in His presence.

text: While David stayed afraid of God, Obed-Edom was being blessed by Him.
explanation:
After Uzzah's death, David didn't seek the Lord to find out where he'd gone wrong. He said, "How can the ark of the Lord come to me?" and kept his distance. That's a slavish fear: the kind Paul says we haven't received again, the spirit of bondage that keeps people away from God.

Meanwhile, a few miles away, the same ark was pouring blessing on a family who welcomed it. God isn't looking for reasons to strike you. He's looking for a heart that will let Him be good to it. True fear of the Lord is like a loved child's reluctance to disappoint parents, and it draws near rather than running away.

text: Obed-Edom was a Gittite, likely a Philistine from Gath. He knew little of the law, but he valued the ark and the blood.
explanation:
Gittite means from Gath, Goliath's city. Some Jewish scholars try to make him a Levite from far-off Gath-rimmon, but David left the ark nearby. David welcomed Gentiles; six hundred men from Gath followed him, and one of them, Ittai, commanded a third of his army.

Amos foretold that when the tabernacle of David was rebuilt, the Gentiles would seek the Lord. Obed-Edom pictures a believer who isn't law-conscious and so isn't sin-conscious, but Jesus-conscious. When the ark moved to Zion, he moved with it, and served as a doorkeeper. "If the ark is leaving, we're following."

text: Obed-Edom's sons and grandsons were "able men": chayil, a word for both strong character and wealth.
explanation:
"God blessed him" with eight sons, and his grandsons "were men of great ability." Sixty-two of his descendants are listed as "able men with strength for the work." The Hebrew chayil describes the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31, and it's also the word for wealth in "it is He who gives you power to get wealth."

The blessing didn't stop at one generation. It was so visible that people reported it to the king: "The Lord has blessed the house of Obed-Edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God." May your household be blessed so evidently that others are drawn to the God you serve.

text: "You should" puts stress on your children. "I believe you will" gives them rest.
explanation:
"You should study more. You shouldn't play so many games. You should…" No one likes being shoulded. The more we say it, the more pressure our children feel, and the law has a way of provoking the very thing it forbids.

You still want change. Then trust God for it, and let your words show it: "I believe you'll do well in this exam. I believe God has given you a heart to study. I believe you'll know when to work and when to play." One way is demand; the other is supply. Speak faith over your children, and watch it draw out what lectures never could.

text: "As your days, so shall your strength be." Your strength can grow along with your years.
explanation:
Moses spoke this blessing over the tribe of Asher. In the natural, life is a steady decline: the older we get, the weaker we become. But God's promise runs against that current: as your days increase, so does your strength.

Caleb lived it. At eighty-five he said, "I am as strong this day as on the day that Moses sent me," when he was forty. If you look at the new year and think, "I'm getting older," receive this promise. "All the promises of God in Him are Yes, and in Him Amen."
